### Also Today
**Setara Launches Daily Index of On-Demand GPU List Prices: HPCwire**
Setara Financial launched the Setara Index, a daily index of on-demand GPU list prices and the first of a planned family of compute benchmarks. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/setara-launches-daily-index-of-on-demand-gpu-list-prices/)

**Tower Semiconductor and Innolight Advance High-Performance Near-Package Optics for AI Infrastructure: Semiconductor Digest**
Tower and Innolight are using Tower's 200-millimetre and 300-millimetre silicon photonics platforms for multiple generations of near-packaged optics aimed at AI infrastructure. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/tower-semiconductor-and-innolight-advance-high-performance-near-package-optics-for-ai-infrastructure/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=tower-semiconductor-and-innolight-advance-high-performance-near-package-optics-for-ai-infrastructure)

**TSMC's acquisition of AUO plant reshapes panel supply chain: digitimes**
Digitimes reports that TSMC's acquisition of an AUO plant is reshaping the panel supply chain. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261104PD212/auo-tsmc-taiwan-plant-lcd-tv-panel.html)

### The Teardown: The Rack That Boils at the Chip
A two-phase direct-to-chip loop picks heat up at the processor by letting liquid boil against a cold plate, then moves that vapor to a condenser, where it gives the heat up and returns as liquid. The phase change is the point. Sensible cooling has to raise the temperature of a flowing liquid to carry energy away. Boiling spends the same energy on latent heat, so a smaller mass of fluid can move a larger load, and the cold plate can sit closer to the silicon than a room full of air ever will. The condenser is still mandatory. Orbit or a data hall, the heat has not left the building until something on the other side of the loop rejects it. In a rack, that something is a coolant distribution unit tied to the facility water or air the building already has.

HPCwire's account of Accelsius's NeuCool IR150 puts that loop in one frame: a fully integrated IT rack plus CDU, which Accelsius calls the industry's first of that kind, offered as shared two-phase infrastructure rather than a chip demo on a bench. The company is a member of the NVIDIA Inception program. It is giving the rack to Villanova University for the National Science Foundation Center for Energy-Smart Electronic Systems, an industry-university cooperative research center. Villanova is one of three university sites in ES2. Accelsius already supports a separate COOLERCHIPS project at the University of Texas at Arlington, led by Dereje Agonafer. Villanova's Laboratory for Advanced Thermal and Fluid Systems is also on the NVIDIA-led OMNICOOL project under ARPA-E's COOLERCHIPS program, and on work with ES2 industry members. Google, Microsoft and Meta are among the industry partners backing ES2.

The worked target is the center's, not a measured result from this donation. ES2's stated objective is to improve the energy efficiency of U.S. data centers by 20 to 35 percent. By the center's own estimate, that is the equivalent of removing one to two power plants every three years. Read that as a program goal attached to a percent band, not as watts this rack has already saved. The IR150 is the instrument for the percent, not the proof of it. Richard Bonner, Accelsius's chief technology officer, framed the gift as research published with the manufacturers building AI infrastructure, not as a finished efficiency claim. Alfonso Ortega, ES2 site director at Villanova, said the donation gives researchers a rack-level view of two-phase direct-to-chip against rising thermal demand. Visitors are invited to the onsite lab. The article's install expectation, early October 2026, sits before the November 3 announcement date, so the useful fact is the partnership and the hardware class, not a calendar you can schedule against.

The integrated two-phase rack stops being the right install when the hall can hold junction temperature with the air or single-phase loop it already runs. The IR150 exists to put a boiling cold plate and a CDU in the same frame so a lab can see the rack, not the chip, as the thermal object. If the cabinet never approaches the load that forced ES2's 20 to 35 percent problem, that frame is a research tool parked in a room that did not need a phase change. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/accelsius-supports-nsf-data-center-efficiency-research-at-villanova/)

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Twenty billion pounds is lined up for up to one gigawatt beside a Yorkshire power station.**

**What You Need to Know:** Brookfield’s estimate for a campus of up to one gigawatt at Drax’s North Yorkshire station is more than twenty billion pounds, with a first phase of up to one hundred megawatts aimed at the first quarter of 2028. The same day’s silicon news is a modeled Arm rack comparison, a one-hundred-fifteen-billion-dollar Marvell–Lumentum agreement, and a DDR5-12800 module from Penguin Solutions. Reported HBM diversion into China, priced around four thousand dollars a stack, is the supply-chain item with a rule attached.

### Top Story
Drax has announced, with Brookfield and Radiant, a plan to develop, deliver and operate data-centre capacity at the 2.6-gigawatt Drax Power Station in Selby, North Yorkshire. Data Center Dynamics reports a phased build: phase one targets up to 100 megawatts and is expected to be operational from the first quarter of 2028; phase two would take capacity to 500 megawatts between 2028 and 2031; phase three envisions further capacity after 2031. Brookfield estimates investment could exceed £20 billion — $26.8 billion in that report, $26.9 billion at BigGo Finance — including an initial £2.5 billion ($3.4 billion) for phase one, through a joint venture with Qatar’s Qai styled Brookfield-Qai AI. Phase one still requires planning, regulatory and network approvals and a tenant; BigGo Finance cites Citi reading the announcement as closer to a memorandum of understanding than a binding contract, with no final investment decision. The proposed site is 1,000 acres with 4 gigawatts of grid access, 2.6 gigawatts of active dispatchable generation, and cooling systems from the existing wood-pellet plant. The UK government had rejected an AI Growth Zone bid for up to 1.2 gigawatts at the same site, and Data Center Dynamics cites Ember putting Drax’s 2025 emissions at 14.1 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/drax-partners-with-brookfield-and-radiant-for-up-to-1gw-data-center-at-north-yorkshire-power-station/) · [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/6bb338b6-8d40-4a09-bd29-9f92ff484914)

### Silicon
**Arm AGI CPU Delivers Nearly 2x Performance per Rack vs x86: Arm**
Arm is promoting an AGI CPU for data centres asked to deliver more compute inside fixed constraints, and says the part was built around performance, scale and efficiency. Independent analysis from Signal65, which Arm highlighted, shows nearly 2x modeled performance per rack for the Arm AGI CPU versus comparable x86 devices. Arm pointed listeners to a Six Five Media discussion of those results with Ryan Shrout, Russ Fellows, Jeff DeFilippi and Ravi Malhotra. Source: [x.com](https://x.com/Arm/status/2117408427810971937) · [x.com](https://x.com/Arm/status/2117433504292045264)

**Marvell Snaps Photonics Chipmaker Lumentum to Bolster AI Connectivity: EE Times**
Marvell has entered a definitive all-stock agreement to acquire Lumentum at an implied value of about $115 billion, pairing interconnect and custom silicon with lasers, optical circuit switching and compound-semiconductor manufacturing. ServeTheHome reports Marvell shareholders would own 67 percent and Lumentum shareholders 33 percent, with three Lumentum directors joining a 10-member board, and that the deal is expected to close in the first half of 2028. Lumentum chief executive Michael Hurlston has called the opening a $550 billion market; Marvell chief executive Matt Murphy said the combination doubles down on supporting Nvidia, which invested $2 billion in each company earlier this year. Lumentum’s indium phosphide process and MEMS optical circuit switches, including the R300, set optical paths without intermediate packet processing. Source: [eetimes.com](https://www.eetimes.com/marvell-snaps-photonics-chipmaker-lumentum-to-bolster-ai-connectivity/) · [servethehome.com](https://www.servethehome.com/marvell-to-acquire-lumentum-115-billion-optical-ai-connectivity/)

**Penguin Solutions Introduces High-Bandwidth SMART Modular MRDIMMs: HPCwire**
Penguin Solutions announced on November 2 a SMART Modular DDR5 multi-ranked DIMM running at DDR5-12800 for AI data centres. The module is offered with optional Zefr testing for reliability. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/penguin-solutions-introduces-high-bandwidth-smart-modular-mrdimms/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Cloud Revenue Hits $168B as AI Capacity Expands: Data Center Knowledge**
Worldwide spending on cloud infrastructure services reached $168 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 55 percent from a year earlier, Synergy Research Group reported. The market has doubled in eight quarters, and AI-specific services now account for roughly one-third of revenue. Chief analyst John Dinsdale told Data Center Knowledge the drivers are capacity coming online, higher pricing, and a shift toward more expensive AI services. JLL figures cited in the same report put hyperscalers at 59 percent of North American data-centre tenant demand, with 28 gigawatts of owner-occupied capacity under construction; neoclouds were 11 percent of demand and AI companies 7 percent. Dell’Oro projects global data-centre capital spending above $3 trillion by 2030. CBRE counted 7,481 megawatts under construction across eight primary North American markets in the first half of 2026, up 24.8 percent, with more than 80 percent preleased, up from 74.3 percent a year earlier. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/cloud/cloud-revenue-hits-168b-as-ai-capacity-expands)

**Putin demands Russian data centers supply capacity to the state: Tom's Hardware**
President Putin has told non-state Russian data centres they must set aside 10 percent of total capacity for the country’s own IT infrastructure after Ukraine drone attacks. Tom’s Hardware reports that slice must be available on 24 hours’ notice. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/putin-demands-russian-data-centers-supply-capacity-to-the-state-in-wake-of-ukraine-drone-attacks-10-percent-capacity-must-be-available-for-state-it-infrastructure-with-24-hours-notice)

**Anthropic signs lease with Australian Data Centres in Western Downs, Queensland: Data Center Dynamics**
Anthropic has signed a lease with Australian Data Centres in Western Downs, Queensland. Australian Data Centres is 85 percent owned by Dexus. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/anthropic-signs-lease-with-australian-data-centres-in-western-downs-queensland/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Smugglers Bypass U.S. Controls to Ship HBM to China: Businesskorea**
The Information, reported on November 2 and carried by Businesskorea, Seoul Economic Daily and Wccftech, describes Korean HBM reaching China inside packages that also carry a low-end server processor, so U.S. rules score the package on the processor rather than the memory; Wccftech traces that opening to December 2024 rules that exempted HBM already integrated into logic products. In China the memory is taken off the board, and failure rates are high because stacks warp or crack, a loss brokers accept because the margin is large. A broker told The Information that one HBM3E, a few hundred dollars a year ago, now trades at about $4,000, and that six to eight stacks on one AI package put memory alone at $24,000 to $32,000. People familiar with Huawei’s supply chain said Huawei told some customers the Ascend 960DT will carry substantial Samsung Electronics and SK hynix HBM, and that Huawei described the chip as twice the performance of existing products. Samsung and SK hynix hold more than 80 percent of the global HBM market, and Huawei has told some customers ordering its AI chips to secure HBM themselves. Source: [businesskorea.co.kr](https://www.businesskorea.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=280371) · [en.sedaily.com](https://en.sedaily.com/international/2026/11/03/smugglers-melt-solder-to-strip-korean-hbm-for-huawei) · [wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/smugglers-hbm-throwaway-server-chips-us-export-controls-loophole-china-south-korea/) · [theinformation.com](https://www.theinformation.com/articles/smugglers-get-expensive-memory-chips-china-south-korea)

**Samsung And TSMC Foundry Cuts Push 8-Inch Chip Capacity Utilisation Towards 90%: Electronics For You BUSINESS**
Samsung and TSMC are cutting 8-inch foundry output. Electronics For You Business reports those cuts are pushing 8-inch chip capacity utilisation towards 90 percent. Source: [electronicsforyou.biz](https://www.electronicsforyou.biz/industry-buzz/samsung-and-tsmc-foundry-cuts-push-8-inch-chip-capacity-utilisation-towards-90/)

### Also Today
**TSMC Has Raised T$14.8 Billion Via Unsecured Bonds: TradingView**
TSMC has raised T$14.8 billion through unsecured bonds. Source: [tradingview.com](https://www.tradingview.com/news/reuters.com,2026:newsml_L3N46K0O2:0-tsmc-has-raised-t-14-8-billion-via-unsecured-bonds/)

**As Samsung and SK hynix rally, three global semiconductor equipment makers add 2,500 workers in South Korea: Fnnews**
Three global semiconductor equipment makers have added 2,500 workers in South Korea as Samsung and SK hynix rally. Source: [en.fnnews.com](https://en.fnnews.com/news/202611031052217411)

**TSMC Eyes Texas Site Near Samsung’s Taylor Chip Plant: Businesskorea**
TSMC is reported to be eyeing a Texas site near Samsung Electronics’ Taylor chip plant, sharpening U.S. foundry competition between the two. Source: [businesskorea.co.kr](https://www.businesskorea.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=280322) · [mt.co.kr](https://www.mt.co.kr/en/industry/2026/11/03/2026110315201193799)

**Hyperscale market shifts: Data Center Dynamics**
An AFL whitepaper says AI workloads are pushing rack power requirements well beyond 100 kilowatts and that cluster fabrics at 800G are part of the physical redesign. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/whitepapers/hyperscale-market-shifts-afl/)

### The Teardown: The Queue Outruns the Hall
New grid infrastructure takes five to fifteen years to build, while a data centre takes one to three, and that mismatch is now visible in how long a project sits between announcement and groundbreaking. Data Center Knowledge, drawing on GlobalData, reports that projects which broke ground between the third quarter of 2025 and the third quarter of 2026 waited an average of just over two years after they were announced. Projects that started construction between early 2020 and mid-2025 waited about eighteen months. The building did not suddenly take six extra months to pour. The clock that moved is the one that starts when a developer has a site and a customer story and ends when someone will actually energize a connection.

An interconnection is a reserved slice of a substation, a line, and a protection scheme, not a cable the tenant can order with the switchgear. Martina Raveni, senior analyst on GlobalData’s Strategic Intelligence team, told Data Center Knowledge the grid is the hardest constraint because it is structural: the line is a five-to-fifteen-year asset and the hall is a one-to-three-year asset. Luis Fernandes, IDC senior research manager for cloud and data centres, went further from his conversations with developers, designers and large operators. He said grid access is the dominant obstacle by a long shot, to the point that his team had not seen projects delayed for any other reason, because the absence of a connection halts the exercise. Other problems — labour, water, local votes — still exist. They only become the binding delay once a connection is real enough that the rest of the schedule can run.

Walk the published intervals against each other. Eighteen months was the older announcement-to-groundbreaking average. Just over two years is the average for the cohort that broke ground across the latest four reported quarters. That is a lengthening of roughly half a year on a clock that is still shorter than either build time in Raveni’s pair. A one-to-three-year hall that is waiting on a five-to-fifteen-year line is not late concrete. It is a project whose useful start date is the energization date of someone else’s asset. In Europe’s main data-centre hubs, Raveni said developers can wait up to a decade for a connection. Set that decade against a one-to-three-year building and the queue is several construction cycles long before the first rack lands. Skilled-labour shortages sit on top of that: insufficient electricians and other trades are pushing some delivery schedules back by around a year, a delay that only starts once the connection exists.

GlobalData’s demand figure shows why the queue does not clear by itself. Annual data-centre electricity consumption is forecast to rise from 590 terawatt-hours in 2025 to 1,520 terawatt-hours in 2030. That is the load the five-to-fifteen-year system is being asked to absorb while halls are still being promised on a one-to-three-year brochure. Investment does not compress a transmission build into a data-centre build. It bids for the connections that already have a date.

On-site gas is the design that looks like a way around the queue. Raveni said it can bridge a power gap, but redundancy requirements may force generating capacity substantially greater than the data centre’s normal needs. The bridge is then larger than the load it serves. Air pollution and water use from that extra plant feed the same local resistance — bills, water, noise, land — that Ya-Han Brownlee-Chen at DP World described as a growing barrier, and Joe Johnston at Xylem tied to power, water and cooling as one infrastructure problem. GlobalData lists closed-loop cooling, water stewardship and diversified power among operator responses, and calls progress uneven.

The gas bridge stops being the right plant when the temporary machines are still burning after the surrounding grid has moved the other way. Raveni’s line is that a temporary fix becomes permanent and pushes emissions up just as grids are decarbonizing. At that point the developer has not escaped the five-to-fifteen-year system. The developer has built a second power station whose size is set by redundancy, not by the IT load, and has inherited the permitting fight the interconnection queue was supposed to avoid. Fernandes, for his part, said there is still no hard evidence that compute capacity itself is limiting AI development. The dated constraint in this account is the connection, not the accelerator. Source: [datacenterknowledge.com](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/energy-power-supply/ai-s-expansion-hits-the-limits-of-local-power)

### On the Horizon
- First quarter of 2028: Drax, Brookfield and Radiant target phase one, up to 100 megawatts, to be operational at Selby, still subject to approvals, a tenant and a final investment decision.
- 2028 through 2031: the same plan schedules a further build toward 500 megawatts, with additional capacity only envisioned after 2031.
- First half of 2028: Marvell’s all-stock acquisition of Lumentum is expected to close.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **A 72-GPU Rubin rack now carries 20.7 terabytes of HBM4 for inference.**

**What You Need to Know:** ASRock Rack showed a Vera Rubin NVL72 at OCP with 20.7 terabytes of HBM4 across 72 GPUs. OpenAI left its Seoul meetings without a new memory contract, while TrendForce sees HBM's blended price more than doubling in 2027. DigiTimes reports Elon Musk is now discussing operational control and joint investment with TSMC on Terafab.

### Top Story
ServeTheHome reports that ASRock Rack showed the XGMRACK-VR/NVL72 at the OCP Global Summit in San Jose: a 48RU NVIDIA MGX rack with 72 Rubin GPUs, 20.7TB of HBM4, a 5000A busbar and a liquid manifold. Inside are 18 Vera Rubin compute trays and nine NVLink 6 switch trays, for 36 NVIDIA Vera CPUs with those GPUs. NVIDIA lists the rack at 3,600 PFLOPS of NVFP4 inference (sparse) and 2,520 PFLOPS of NVFP4 training (dense), and each Rubin GPU gets 288GB of HBM4. Power comes from four 3RU shelves rated at 110kW each, using six 18.3kW supplies plus bulk capacitors; cooling-distribution options are in-rack, in-row, rear-door heat exchanger, or a liquid-to-air sidecar. Each compute tray is liquid-cooled, with eight 800Gbps OSFP ports from ConnectX-9 SuperNICs and two 400Gbps QSFP112 ports from a BlueField-4 DPU. Source: [servethehome.com](https://www.servethehome.com/liquid-cooled-nvidia-servers-at-the-asrock-rack-ocp-2026-booth/)

### Silicon
**Xeon 6 leads a recorded agent-workload bake-off: Intel**
Intel says a Xeon 6 processor-based instance delivered 1.66 times the normalized agent-task throughput of a 5th Gen AMD EPYC instance and 4.5 times an Arm v9.2A instance on a healthcare Terminal-Bench trace. The comparison ran at 24-way concurrency for 60 minutes with identical code, inputs and agent trajectories. A record-and-replay method held the workflow fixed so the gap is attributed to the platform rather than to changing tool choices. The healthcare set included clinical documentation, evidence retrieval, fraud detection and laboratory diagnostics, among other tasks. The write-up is by Nithya Rao and Saumya Buliya of Intel. Source: [t.co](https://t.co/21eeu6lx9B)

**AI Reshapes Memory Architecture as Macronix Expands Flash Portfolio: EE Times**
Martin Lin, Macronix marketing director, told EE Times Taiwan that AI is changing memory architecture, not only memory demand. Macronix raised 2026 capital expenditure to NT$37.8 billion to expand 12-inch wafer capacity for 3D NOR, NAND, eMMC and related products. Lin said a previous-generation rack used about 600 to 800 NOR flash devices and the latest generation has more than 1,000, for boot, firmware, control and security as controller and switch counts rise. Market data in the piece put the memory market above $20 billion in 2025 and near $70 billion in 2026, with NOR flash, SLC NAND and low-capacity eMMC together around $24 billion in 2026. The article describes high-bandwidth flash, built on 3D NAND, as a higher-capacity tier for data that does not have to stay in HBM, and says equipment install, qualification and yield ramp can take two to three years. Source: [eetimes.com](https://www.eetimes.com/ai-reshapes-memory-architecture-as-macronix-expands-flash-portfolio/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Musk outlines Colossus 2 halls at roughly 220,000 Blackwell GPUs each: Wccftech**
Wccftech reports that Elon Musk shared plans, so this is announced rather than energized, for Colossus 2 halls named Macroharder, Minihard and Gun Range, each with roughly 220,000 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Source: [wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/elon-musk-rumored-to-soften-stance-on-tsmc-for-terafab-after-calling-it-a-subcontractor-at-best-with-operational-control-and-joint-investment-on-the-table/)

**The Datacenter Backlash Goes Bipartisan: SemiAnalysis**
SemiAnalysis says the 2027 US data-centre buildout is largely locked in, while a prolonged Texas permit freeze is now the biggest single risk to 2028, and that both parties are running on tighter rules. Source: [newsletter.semianalysis.com](https://newsletter.semianalysis.com/p/the-datacenter-backlash-goes-bipartisan)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**OpenAI seeks memory and cash in Seoul, and leaves without a new contract: ET CIO**
ET CIO, citing The Korea Herald, reports that OpenAI chief Sam Altman met about 50 Samsung executives in Yongin on Saturday and then SK Group chairman Chey Tae-won with SK hynix and SK Telecom executives, and that no new supply or investment agreements were announced. Altman, as carried by that report, said simply using AI will no longer be enough to secure a sustainable competitive advantage. TrendForce forecasts that HBM's blended average selling price could rise 121 percent in 2027 from 2026. Samsung said its HBM supply for 2027 is sold out; SK hynix said output through 2029 is effectively accounted for through firm contracts and volumes under negotiation, and HBM sales head Kim Ki-tae said customers are requesting more than twice the volume the company can supply. The Herald says OpenAI has reportedly secured about $11 billion in commitments against an initial $30 billion target — figures not independently confirmed — and that the October 2025 Stargate outline of demand equivalent to 900,000 DRAM wafer starts a month was a production target, not a binding order. International Business Times, citing The Wall Street Journal, adds that a hoped-for valuation fell to about $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and that the raise was later cut to a target of as much as $20 billion. Source: [cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com](https://cio.economictimes.indiatimes.com/news/data-center/openai-seeks-crucial-partnerships-with-samsung-and-sk-amid-memory-chip-supply-crisis/135450132?utm_source=portal_category_widget&utm_medium=homepage)

**Musk may cede Terafab control to TSMC, Digitimes reports: Wccftech**
After earlier casting TSMC as a subcontractor at best, Musk is reported by DigiTimes, via Wccftech, to be renegotiating, with operational control and joint investment on the table, including advanced packaging. TSMC chief C.C. Wei said on the latest earnings call that the firm was in discussions with Musk and would have to run the plants for any deal to work. The Terafab concept, as described in the report, envisions more than a terawatt of computing capacity. The account is a report of talks, not a signed contract. Source: [wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/elon-musk-rumored-to-soften-stance-on-tsmc-for-terafab-after-calling-it-a-subcontractor-at-best-with-operational-control-and-joint-investment-on-the-table/)

**TSMC's Arizona Plant Creates Magnet Effect: BigGo Finance**
BigGo Finance reports TSMC's cumulative Arizona investment has reached $265 billion, including an additional $100 billion announced this year, which the piece calls the largest foreign investment on record in the United States. The first fab is operational. TSMC employs about 3,500 people in Arizona and plans to hire 2,500 more. Colliers figures in the article show industrial vacancy in the northwestern Phoenix cluster fell from 16 percent a year earlier to 8 percent in June. Zillow data cited there put six-year home-price gains in North Gateway and Desert View at about 53 percent, against 42 percent for Phoenix overall, and after TSMC took about 900 acres in NorthPark the planned residential scale there was cut by about 20 percent. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/7dcaced9-e490-4c00-99e8-4e9db84a6976)

### Also Today
**Ace nanochem Develops Three New Semiconductor Materials for Power Devices and Advanced Packaging: Yahoo Finance**
Yahoo Finance reports that Ace nanochem has developed three new semiconductor materials aimed at power devices and advanced packaging. Source: [finance.yahoo.com](https://finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/ace-nanochem-develops-three-semiconductor-000000345.html)

### The Teardown: When the Old Well Still Pumps
A token is the barrel. Each GPU generation is a well. EE Times, walking through a Gartner forecast and an a16z rental chart, treats the cost of that barrel as mostly energy plus whether the chip can do the job at all. Easy wells — newer silicon that finishes more work per watt — stay open when the token price falls. Hard wells shut first. Rent sitting above a depreciation line does not make the well profitable: power, cooling, networking, the building and the cost of borrowing still come out.

Gartner's arithmetic, as EE Times reports it, starts with providers spending close to $1 trillion on AI infrastructure in 2026 and another $6 trillion from 2027 through 2030. To pay for that spend, cover borrowing, and still earn a 12 percent return, the owners of those data centers would need about $8.5 trillion in revenue through 2030. Gartner expects the AI revenue that actually reaches those data centers to be $3.6 trillion at most. The gap is what Gartner calls more than $3.5 trillion of spending that could be exposed to write-downs by 2030. EE Times is careful: that is a risk estimate under Gartner's assumptions, not a prediction that the full amount will be written off. On the same arithmetic, more than 80 percent of neoclouds would no longer exist as independent companies.

Set that against the price of the work. Epoch AI, as cited in the piece, estimates that the price of reaching a given benchmark score has fallen by roughly 13 times a year since 2023, on the benchmarks it tracks. Cheaper tokens can pull in new jobs — the Jevons pattern, where a lower cost per use raises total use — but nothing in the chart guarantees that demand grows faster than the price falls. If use only doubles while the price of a scored result drops thirteenfold, revenue still shrinks.

The rental chart is the field log. a16z, using Ornn data as of October 19, drew a straight line from each Nvidia generation's first observed rent down to zero over six years, about the period hyperscalers use to write the servers off. Every generation was renting above that line. The H200 sat 143 percent above it. EE Times notes that most of the gap opened after April, when token demand took off, and that for most of their lives these chips had rented below the line. A busy well can still lose money once the power bill is paid.

The oil picture breaks where tokens are not the same crude. Interactive and agent work wants low latency and the newest memory. Overnight document work, synthetic data and evaluations mostly want a low cost per token and barely notice delay. A chip whose capital is already written off, with power, cooling and upkeep left as the main costs, can be the cheapest barrel for that second market. There is not one token price. There are at least two.

Keeping every generation online stops being the right call when a newer generation is arriving in volume and the token price has fallen far enough that an unpaid-off older chip's energy cost exceeds what even the latency-blind jobs will pay. Until that crossover, the expensive well still pumps, because the alternative is turning away work the new wells cannot yet absorb. Source: [eetimes.com](https://www.eetimes.com/jevon-paradox-and-the-silicon-roadmap/)

### On the Horizon
- Macronix expects NOR flash, SLC NAND and eMMC prices to rise further in the third and fourth quarters of 2026, then stabilize at elevated levels.
- Two further TSMC Arizona fabs are expected to be completed by 2030.
- Microsoft plans to scale its own Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, claiming 40 percent more tokens per megawatt, a figure EE Times says is not independently verified.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Seven point three billion dollars of quarterly data-center revenue still leaves Intel short of Xeon demand.**

**What You Need to Know:** Intel's data-center and AI business booked $7.3 billion in the third quarter of 2026, up 17% from the prior quarter and nearly 80% from a year earlier, and the company is still short of Xeon supply. It is converting some Oregon Intel 18A wafer capacity to Intel 3 for Xeon 6 Granite Rapids, with that added Intel 3 output expected in the second half of 2027. Samsung's chairman was in the Yokohama packaging lab the same weekend, and the locked Vera Rubin sheet is what production hardware is shipping against.

### Top Story
Intel is reallocating leading-edge wafer tools from client chips to server CPUs because data-center demand is outrunning what the lines can ship. On the third-quarter 2026 earnings call, CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the industry is navigating one of the most significant supply shortages in history, driven by demand for what he called Super Intelligence, and that server supply grew in the quarter while later quarters will still struggle to keep pace. The Data Center and AI business generated $7.3 billion, up 17% sequentially and nearly 80% year over year. CFO Dave Zinsner said wafers being taken offline in Oregon are Intel 18A wafers that generally go to Panther Lake; weaker PC demand, which Intel expects to last at least through the first half of next year, frees some of that capacity for data-center wafers. Those tools will run Intel 3, the node behind Xeon 6 Granite Rapids. Tan said the added Intel 3 capacity should be in production in the second half of 2027. Intel 3 manufacturing costs have fallen about 15% since the first quarter of 2026. Granite Rapids is already the company's fastest-ramping server family, and management says demand still exceeds supply. Intel expects data-center CPU demand to stay strong in 2027 and 2028 as operators deploy more CPU-heavy agentic and inference work. Fab 24 near Leixlip, Ireland, is being expanded for more Xeon output, with that capacity online by the end of 2027 unless the move is accelerated. In Arizona, Intel 18A is ramping at Fab 52, and equipment installation into adjacent Fab 62 has been pulled forward; Fab 62 is set to be the second high-volume site for 18A, 18A-P, and derivatives. Intel also bought tools aggressively in the third quarter and said it expects to take some client share with Core Ultra 400-series Nova Lake, which will need high-volume 18A and 18A-P wafers. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-shifts-production-capacity-from-consumer-to-server-cpus-in-face-of-unprecedented-ai-demand-company-navigating-one-of-the-most-significant-supply-shortages-in-history)

### Silicon
**Samsung chairman highlights chip packaging, visits Japanese unit: The Korea Times**
Samsung Electronics executive chairman Lee Jae-yong visited the Advanced Package Lab in Yokohama on Sunday and said the company will keep expanding the research workforce there and turn the lab into a global R&D hub for next-generation packaging. He discussed materials and process work with researchers and ways to tighten cooperation with Japan's materials, parts, and equipment industry. Samsung says advanced packaging is now critical for AI processor chips because it integrates several dies, including GPUs and high-bandwidth memory, in one package. APL was established in 2023 and held its official opening in September this year. Starting in 2024, Samsung has been investing 40 billion yen, about $254 million, over five years in the Japan research infrastructure. The lab develops and validates packaging materials and processes and is meant to sit between Samsung's design and manufacturing and Japanese suppliers. Its research areas differ from the packaging unit at the Semiconductor R&D Center in Korea; the two groups plan to work together. APL's next scope includes wafer bonding, glass substrates, and new high-performance packaging architectures aimed at energy-efficient parts in volume. Source: [koreatimes.co.kr](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20261101/samsung-chairman-highlights-chip-packaging-visits-japanese-unit)

**NVIDIA Updates Rubin GPU Specs as First Production Hardware Arrives: ServeTheHome**
With the first Vera Rubin NVL72 systems being made generally available to hyperscaler customers, NVIDIA has locked shipping specifications below the preliminary bandwidth targets and above the preliminary scale-out figures. A single Rubin GPU is now listed at 19.2 TB/s of HBM4, not the 22 TB/s target, which ServeTheHome calculates as about 9.375 Gbps per pin across eight stacks versus about 10.75 Gbps per pin before, a drop of about 1.375 Gbps per pin, or roughly 11%. The official HBM4 rate cited in that account is 8 Gbps per pin on a bus widened from 1,024 bits to 2,048 bits per stack. NVLink scale-up per GPU is 3.0 TB/s, down from 3.6 TB/s. Scale-out networking per GPU is 450 GB/s, up from 400 GB/s. Memory capacity is unchanged at 288 GB per GPU. Paper compute is unchanged at 50 PFLOPS of FP4 inference and 35 PFLOPS of FP4 training. On the NVL72 rack, aggregate GPU memory bandwidth is 1,400 TB/s, down from 1,580 TB/s, and scale-up bandwidth is 216 TB/s, down from 260 TB/s, while scale-out networking is 32.4 TB/s bidirectional, up from 28.8 TB/s. Rack HBM4 capacity stays at 20.7 TB. AMD's MI455X, in the same account, runs HBM4 at 7.6 Gbps per pin, so NVIDIA's revised rate is still above that rival's. TechRadar, comparing pages and a Wayback window, places the quiet edit between September 1 and September 11, after August results that already had Vera Rubin racks running at CoreWeave, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Source: [servethehome.com](https://www.servethehome.com/nvidia-updates-rubin-gpu-specs-as-first-production-hardware-arrives/)

### Data Centres & Power
**Measuring the environmental impact of delivering AI at Google Scale: arXiv**
Google's published full-stack measurement of Gemini Apps puts the median text prompt at 0.24 watt-hours, 0.03 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent, and 0.26 milliliters of water. The method counts active AI accelerator power, host system energy, idle machine capacity, and data-center energy overhead, not accelerator draw alone. The same paper says software efficiency work and clean-energy procurement cut energy for that median prompt 33 times and the carbon footprint 44 times over one year. Google's infrastructure blog equates the 0.24 watt-hours to watching television for less than nine seconds. Source: [arxiv.org](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.15734)

**Power Costs for Data Centers Across the U.S.: 2026 Edition: Site Selection Group**
A site-selection analysis dated August 11, 2026, says power still represents up to 70% of a data center's operating costs, but availability now often matters more than the cents per kilowatt-hour. It cites Gartner's June 2026 forecast of 565 terawatt-hours of data-center electricity use this year, a 26% jump from 447 terawatt-hours in 2025. The piece frames AI demand since 2023 as the driver, and treats "can the megawatts be had, and how long is the wait" as the binding question for many projects. Source: [info.siteselectiongroup.com](https://info.siteselectiongroup.com/blog/power-costs-for-data-centers-across-the-u.s.-2026-edition)

**Apple Takes Back the Top Spot From NVIDIA After Rough Day for AI Stocks: TechPowerUp**
The same Friday session that reordered market caps also carried an operating fact about who is funding the build: Alphabet and Amazon have seen free cash flow turn negative, and that gap is pushing them toward debt markets to pay for AI data-center outlays. NVIDIA, as the main supplier of AI GPUs, is tied to those budgets. Apple, which the account says has largely stayed out of the AI infrastructure race, is the contrast on cash, not the capacity story. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354347/apple-takes-back-the-top-spot-from-nvidia-after-rough-day-for-ai-stocks)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**Intel shifts production capacity from consumer to server CPUs: Tom's Hardware**
Wafers are not the only shortage on the Xeon ramp. Zinsner said Intel is constrained on the substrate side as well as the wafer side, because multi-chiplet server packages need advanced organic substrates. Intel has been working with substrate suppliers and expects about 40% more substrate capacity in the second half of 2027. It is also expanding advanced packaging in New Mexico and Malaysia for internal products and external customers. Granite Rapids already uses EMIB to connect compute dies. Clearwater Forest combines EMIB with Foveros Direct 3D and hybrid bonding, stacking Intel 18A compute dies on Intel 3 base dies. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-shifts-production-capacity-from-consumer-to-server-cpus-in-face-of-unprecedented-ai-demand-company-navigating-one-of-the-most-significant-supply-shortages-in-history)

**Samsung chairman highlights chip packaging, visits Japanese unit: The Korea Times**
Samsung says it put APL in Japan because the country holds a deep set of materials, parts, and equipment companies and a working link among industry, academia, and research institutes. The company also pointed to the Japanese government having designated semiconductors and AI as strategic sectors and pursuing investment and support, which Samsung called a reason Japan is an attractive R&D hub for local partnerships. The Yokohama plan is to use that talent pool and connect Japanese materials and equipment suppliers to Samsung's process capability. Source: [koreatimes.co.kr](https://www.koreatimes.co.kr/business/companies/20261101/samsung-chairman-highlights-chip-packaging-visits-japanese-unit)

### The Teardown: A Word That Is Two Bytes
A PDP-11 memory transaction is a word, not a byte, and the lowest address bit is a lane select rather than part of the location the memory board is allowed to treat as a full address. Dave Plummer, building a replacement board because a megabyte of period memory for his machine was priced in too many zeros, ran into that rule the hard way. Tom's Hardware reports the project: a Q-bus card, a Lattice MachXO2 FPGA as the memory controller, four ISSI 1 MB chips, a U2S I/O chip, DIP switches, comm ports, and capacitors, tested on a backplane beside an M8190 CPU board.

The bus is 22 bits wide. The M8190 design reserves the top 256 KB for I/O and ROM, so not every address the 22 bits can name is RAM the CPU may use as main memory. Later PDP-11 models could take as much as four megabytes. Four 1 MB chips are four megabytes of physical storage on the card, which matches that ceiling on paper and then has to obey the word rule in the controller.

On a read, the CPU may want one byte, but the controller still has to return a whole word, two bytes. The low bit tells the CPU which lane, low byte or high byte, it will keep. On a write, the same bit has to be decoded before the store. The bus still carries a full word. If the controller writes both bytes, the lane the CPU did not mean to touch gets whatever else was on the bus. Plummer's first controller returned every second word. A commenter on the account joked that he had built 4 MB of memory that turned out to be 2 MB. That is the failure mode in one sentence: the array was sized for four megabytes, and the address decode treated the lane bit as a word address, so half the locations never participated in a legal transaction.

The fix sits in the FPGA, not in a respin of the ISSI chips. Reads always present both bytes. Writes mask to the selected byte and leave the other byte in the word alone. Plummer had not flash-programmed an FPGA before this board; that was a separate bring-up loop, and it is not the same bug. The lane bug is a protocol mismatch between a modern byte-oriented mental model and a 1970 machine whose memory bus never offered a byte strobe the way a later DRAM controller would.

He had already sidestepped the whole class of problem a week earlier with a QBone DEC interface that carries a Beaglebone Black and implements the memory in software on the far side of the bus. That works, and it is a different product: a single-board computer pretending to be Q-bus RAM, not four discrete megabyte chips behind a small FPGA. The discrete board is the right shape when the goal is a period-correct card that the M8190 can cycle as if the chips were of the era. It stops being the right shape when the controller cannot guarantee a byte lane mask on every write. At that point the software path on the QBone is the one that cannot corrupt the untouched half of the word, because the lane select is handled in code before any store, and the four ISSI chips are no longer in the path at all. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/ram/veteran-microsoft-engineer-makes-his-own-ram-from-scratch-using-ai-attempts-to-build-4mb-of-1970s-pdp-11-ram-from-scratch)

### On the Horizon
- Second half of 2027: Intel's added Intel 3 capacity in Oregon is slated to enter production for Xeon 6.
- End of 2027: expanded Xeon capacity at Fab 24 in Leixlip, Ireland, is slated to come online unless Intel accelerates it.
- Second half of 2027: Intel expects about 40% more advanced organic substrate capacity from suppliers.
- March 2027: Samsung SDS plans a Vera Rubin GPU-as-a-service launch, as reported alongside the revised Rubin sheet.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **Six hundred million dollars is what a two-week Fab 28 halt costs Intel in server-chip revenue.**

**What You Need to Know:** Six hundred million dollars is what Intel expects to lose across two quarters after a two-week shutdown at Fab 28 near Kiryat Gat, almost all of it in 10-nanometer-class server chips. The same reporting window has Sherman named as a leading candidate for a further TSMC fab search, and Google buying land in Hamina while Finnish projects of 50 megawatts and 40 megawatts move in opposite directions. A lab optical switch from PsiQuantum is already inside the loss budget data-center links allow.

### Top Story
**Intel Fab 28 Shutdown to Cost $600 Million in Lost Revenue, Production to Restart Soon: TechPowerUp**
An explosion in mid-October at Intel’s Fab 28 near Kiryat Gat, Israel, killed two people and seriously injured one, and the fab has been shut for about two weeks. Chief financial officer David Zinsner said Intel expects to start production again by the end of this week while it sorts which wafers still in the line are usable. He put the revenue hit at about $300 million in the fourth quarter of 2026 and a similar $300 million in the first quarter of 2027 — about $600 million across the two quarters — and said almost all of the fourth-quarter figure is 10-nanometer server product. Tom’s Hardware reports the accident is also expected to cut fourth-quarter non-GAAP gross margin by about 2 percent, with most wafer write-offs landing in that quarter even though shipments stay disrupted into early 2027. Xeon 6 still uses Intel 7 input-output dies, and Intel still sells Xeon 5 Emerald Rapids on Intel 7; it stopped taking orders for Xeon 4 Sapphire Rapids in late September. Other 10-nanometer-capable fabs, including lines in Arizona, cannot fully cover the gap while server demand is already tight, and Intel has not said it will move Xeon 6 input-output production onto lines used for older CPUs. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354327/intel-fab-28-shutdown-to-cost-usd-600-million-in-lost-revenue-production-to-restart-soon) · [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/deadly-intel-fab-28-explosion-causes-two-week-shutdown-to-cost-usd600-million-and-severely-disrupt-server-chip-manufacturing-for-six-months-10nm-xeon-shipments-stall-during-largest-shortage-in-memory)

### Silicon
**Intel Q3 2026 Earnings Data Center Soars While PC Faces Memory Pressure: ServeTheHome**
Intel’s third-quarter 2026 revenue was $16.5 billion, up 21 percent year over year, with non-GAAP gross margin at 44.1 percent. Data Center and AI revenue was $7.3 billion, up 78 percent — David Zinsner called that the strongest data-center revenue growth in 15 years — and segment operating income was $3.0 billion at a 41.5 percent margin. “Purpose Built Silicon” revenue more than doubled, and CEO Lip-Bu Tan said the immediate priority is unlocking supply for Xeon; on the call he said substrate availability is limiting output and will take time to ease. Client Computing and Physical AI revenue fell 5 percent to $8.1 billion as higher DRAM and NAND prices lift system cost. TechPowerUp reports Intel expects the PC market to shrink about 12 percent in units this year and sees another 10 percent decline in 2027, with the PC slowdown continuing at least through the first half of next year and memory pricing pressure persisting into 2027. Intel Foundry revenue was $6.7 billion, up 58 percent including intersegment sales, with an operating loss of $1.9 billion versus $2.3 billion a year earlier; the Intel 14A 0.9 process design kit was released in October, Ohio expansion continues, and the call indicated 18A supply is being looked at for the data-center side pending substrate. Source: [servethehome.com](https://www.servethehome.com/intel-q3-2026-earnings-data-center-foundry-client/) · [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354340/intel-data-center-revenue-jumps-78-but-weak-q4-guidance-drags-stock-down-30)

**GIGABYTE Advances Local AI Infrastructure with WRX90 AI TOP Motherboard: TechPowerUp**
GIGABYTE announced the WRX90 AI TOP workstation motherboard for AMD Ryzen Threadripper PRO processors, aimed at on-premises local AI workloads. It has seven PCIe 5.0 x16 slots and two MCIO 8i connectors, which GIGABYTE says can support up to nine GPU devices through compatible expansion hardware. Eight-channel DDR5 supports up to 2 TB of ECC RDIMM, and the board includes enterprise-grade BMC remote management. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354325/gigabyte-advances-local-ai-infrastructure-with-wrx90-ai-top-motherboard)

**PsiQuantum Turns Its Photonics Know-How into an Optical Switch for AI Data Center GPU Networks: Tom's Hardware**
Tom’s Hardware reports PsiQuantum has turned its photonics work into an optical switch aimed at AI data-center GPU networks. The eight-port device typically loses 1.2 dB — under a quarter of its light — against a data-center allowance of up to 3 dB. The 8x8 unit is a lab prototype, and the company plans larger devices. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/photonics/psiquantum-turns-its-photonics-know-how-into-an-optical-switch-for-supercharging-ai-data-center-gpu-networks-8x8-lab-prototype-loses-less-light-than-rivals-with-plans-to-develop-larger-devices)

### Data Centres & Power
**Google Buys 56 Hectares in Hamina, Finland, Amid Ongoing Issues over Muhos Tree-Felling: Data Center Dynamics**
Google has bought 56 hectares in Hamina, Finland. Tom’s Hardware reports a criminal investigation into environmental damage tied to Google’s Finnish subsidiary, after local police acted on complaints about breaches of environmental law connected to tree-felling at Muhos. In the same Finland roundup, Tekova plans an announced 50-megawatt data center in Perho, and SRV has backed out of a 40-megawatt project in Eura. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/google-buys-56-hectares-in-hamina-finland-amid-ongoing-issues-over-muhos-tree-felling/) · [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/criminal-investigation-launched-into-googles-ai-data-center-deforestation-in-finland-local-police-act-over-multiple-complaints-about-breaches-of-environmental-law)

**PowerBank Plans 2MW Modular Data Center in Ontario, Canada: Data Center Dynamics**
PowerBank’s 2-megawatt modular data center in Ontario, Canada, is announced. The company has signed a first lease with an AI cloud partner. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/powerbank-plans-2mw-modular-data-center-in-ontario-canada/)

**DayOne Signs MoU with Sembcorp and Inks MoU with Blue Whale Energy: Data Center Dynamics**
DayOne has signed a memorandum of understanding with Sembcorp to integrate power and energy solutions across Asia-Pacific data centers, as part of DayOne’s Bring Your Own Power initiative. A separate memorandum with Blue Whale Energy will explore whether a distributed virtual power plant in Singapore is feasible, in support of DayOne’s SG1 data center. Both are memoranda, not energized supply. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/dayone-signs-mou-with-sembcorp-to-integrate-power-and-energy-solutions-across-apac-data-centers/) · [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/dayone-inks-mou-with-blue-whale-energy-to-explore-feasibility-of-a-distributed-virtual-power-plant-in-singapore/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**From Fire Watch to Fab Tools: The First Graduates of an ASU Program Built for TSMC Arizona: Digital Information World**
TSMC Arizona employs more than 3,500 people in north Phoenix and has projected 6,000 employees to support its first three fabs. AZ Big Media, after the October 15 earnings call, reported that construction of the second fab is now complete within a site investment that now totals $265 billion, and that construction is well underway on the third fab. TSMC Arizona expects to fill more than 100 equipment technician positions by the end of 2026, with plans for hundreds more equipment, facilities, process, and manufacturing technician roles before the end of 2030. Arizona State University’s Foundations for Equipment Technician Program, built with TSMC Arizona, graduated its first two cohorts in late July; many participants already held full-time offers, the course is free to the student, and a successful graduate is guaranteed an interview. Each format is about 168 hours across nine topic areas and three professional certificates. Grand Canyon University’s 11-week manufacturing specialist program, launched with TSMC in 2025, has trained about 100 students, with an 83 percent completion rate, and roughly 70 percent of graduates have received offers; TSMC’s registered equipment-technician apprenticeship runs 12 to 18 months. Source: [digitalinformationworld.com](https://www.digitalinformationworld.com/2026/10/from-fire-watch-to-fab-tools-first.html)

**Sherman Is Likely Contender for TSMC Semiconductor Expansion: Bisnow**
Bisnow reports Sherman has been identified as the leading candidate for TSMC’s next fabrication plant, which the Dallas Business Journal reported could bring a $120 billion investment. State documents the Journal obtained describe an unnamed semiconductor manufacturer seeking Texas sites for a $45 billion investment in two plants, while Bloomberg has reported TSMC considering the Dallas-Fort Worth area for as many as six facilities at $20 billion each. On the October 15 earnings call, CEO C.C. Wei said U.S. customers have asked TSMC to expand beyond Phoenix and that nearly 20 fabs worldwide are in progress. Sherman officials said the city has not been contacted. Sherman has already lined up more than $40 billion from Texas Instruments, GlobalWafers, and Coherent, and land broker Rex Glendenning told the Journal the city’s water volume is the only supply he knows in the market that can feed that kind of plant. The Austin Business Journal reported Central Texas is also being considered. Source: [bisnow.com](https://www.bisnow.com/news/dallas-ft-worth/industrial/taiwan-semiconductor-manufacturing-co-could-expand-in-north-texas)

**OpenAI CEO Says It's 'Quite Terrible' for Your PC to Have RAM: Tom's Hardware**
In a podcast interview reported by Tom’s Hardware, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said it is “quite terrible” for people to have RAM in their own PCs when that memory could go into AI data centers, which he said offer better utilization. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/openai-ceo-says-its-quite-terrible-for-your-pc-to-have-ram-sam-altman-says-data-centers-offer-better-utilization)

### The Teardown: The Motor That Cannot Just Swap the Magnet
A factory-automation motor stores part of its magnetic field in a permanent magnet, so the drive does not have to create that field from current on every cycle. The way to take it apart is to ask what the current, the steel, and the control loop have to replace if the magnet is no longer allowed to do that job. Asia Business Daily, translating Taiwan’s Economic Daily News, reports that TSMC has asked suppliers whether rare-earth-free motors could be used in factory automation equipment, and is putting components that use rare earths into its equipment supply-chain review.

Those magnets sit in the same class of material China restricted in April 2025: samarium, gadolinium, terbium, dysprosium, lutetium, scandium, and yttrium — seven elements. The report describes them as key inputs to high-performance permanent magnets used in electric vehicles, robots, and industrial automation, which is why a wafer fab’s handling and positioning motors are now on the same watch list as a robot joint. In October 2025 the controls were widened on paper toward more rare earths and toward permanent-magnet manufacturing technology. Some of those wider measures were postponed. The April 2025 list was not.

Swapping the magnet is not the design. The same report says efficiency, torque, control performance, and reliability all have to meet semiconductor-equipment requirements. A reluctance motor — the approach Shuo Yang is exploring for industrial equipment and for cooling systems in AI data centers — makes torque because a shaped rotor is pulled into the low-reluctance path of a rotating stator field. No rare-earth magnet, so none of those seven elements in the rotor. The stator still needs electrical steel, which is the materials path China Steel is pursuing, and a current waveform precise enough to keep torque smooth, which is why Fukuta’s motor-design work belongs in the same cluster as a drive specialist. In a tool bay, ripple and heat are process risks: a missed step or extra heat in the wrong enclosure is a defect, not a comfort complaint. That is the control-performance bar, and it is why the response is a materials company, a motor company, and a drive approach together, not a single magnet vendor.

The only capacity figures in the report are for a domestic materials line, not for a motor. The Industrial Technology Research Institute runs a rare-earth pilot line and, with government support, is moving a separate demonstration plant targeted for completion by the end of 2028, with annual production of 500 tons of rare earths by the end of 2030. The government plans to use that output to meet about 50 percent of the island’s domestic demand. At the stated 2030 rate, half of demand is still outside the new plant even if the tonnage lands on target. A design that still needs any of the seven April 2025 elements stays inside a licensing regime that is already live. The 500-ton plan does not retire that exposure; it only describes how much of a magnet-based chain Taiwan hopes to feed locally, and the stated share is about half.

The rare-earth-free motor stops being the right substitution when it cannot meet efficiency, torque, control performance, and reliability together on the tool. At that point the actuator stays on a permanent-magnet motor, and the supply plan is inventory plus a license, not a rotor redraw. The demonstration plant does not move that test. It only changes how much magnet material a design that failed the test could hope to source on the island. Source: [asiae.co.kr](https://www.asiae.co.kr/en/article/2026103008563538885)

### On the Horizon
- Some expanded Chinese rare-earth control measures announced in October 2025 stay postponed until November 10, 2026; the April 2025 controls remain in place.
- Arizona State University plans to run up to 12 additional equipment-technician cohorts a year through 2028.

# AI Chips & Data Centres Daily
> **TSMC is weighing a twenty percent CoWoS price hike as packaging stays tight.**

**What You Need to Know:** TSMC is weighing a twenty percent price increase on CoWoS while AI demand keeps advanced packaging tight. Intel is pulling 18A wafers off Panther Lake so it can build more Granite Rapids. A 700-megawatt data centre is proposed outside Lansing, and SpaceX is reported to be buying 418 nearby homes only if owners drop a lawsuit.

### Top Story
Semiconductor Engineering’s week in review says TSMC is considering a 20 percent price increase for CoWoS as AI demand continues to strain advanced-packaging capacity. The same review says ASE forecasts a doubling of its advanced-packaging revenue in 2027. Amkor is ramping new high-density fan-out and 2.5D packaging programs. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-162/)

### Silicon
**Intel pulls Panther Lake wafers for Granite Rapids: Tom's Hardware**
Tom's Hardware reports that Intel is taking 18A wafers that had been going to Panther Lake offline, freeing that capacity so Oregon can put Intel 3 in and build more Granite Rapids data-centre CPUs. Nova Lake, already on the client roadmap, is now confirmed by CEO Lip-Bu Tan as the first 18A-P client product and is tracking ahead of schedule. Design wins at launch are expected to be twice those of Panther Lake, with more detail at CES in January. Against 18A, 18A-P is a 9 percent speed gain at the same power, or an 18 percent power cut at the same speed, and Intel has described it as a drop-in for 18A designs. Demand for Wildcat Lake is outstripping supply. Intel expects its client business to decline by more than 20 percent next quarter, and the 2026 PC-unit market to decline about 12 percent. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/pc-components/cpus/intel-confirms-nova-lake-will-use-advanced-18a-p-node-more-details-at-ces-company-says-its-taking-panther-lake-capacity-offline-to-build-more-granite-rapids-data-center-cpus)

**SK hynix creates a US Americas chief post: BigGo Finance**
SK hynix has created a president-level Americas organization based in the United States and named development chief Ahn Hyun to lead it, effective November 1. Ahn has led AI memory development, including HBM and SOCAMM. The role is to build a response system around US big-tech customers and to strengthen technology leadership and R&D. Cha Sun-yong takes the development post while continuing as head of the Future Technology Research Institute. Yoon Poong-young moves to head the Corporate Center, and CEO Kwak Noh-jung stays after six consecutive record quarters. Source: [finance.biggo.com](https://finance.biggo.com/news/bfcad863-99fa-46ae-ab33-c71c149458e5)

**Hanmi Semiconductor receives an SK hynix plaque: Chosunbiz**
Hanmi Semiconductor said on October 30 that it received a plaque from SK hynix for HBM equipment and mass-production support. The companies have worked together since a 2015 thermocompression bonder, and cumulative equipment sales to SK hynix over ten years are about 600 billion won. In 2017 Hanmi developed Korea’s first dual TC bonder, which it says roughly doubled productivity versus earlier tools, and the two companies jointly won the IR52 Jang Young Sil Award. TC bonders have supported SK hynix from HBM2 through HBM3, HBM3E and HBM4, including HBM supplied to NVIDIA. Hanmi runs offices in Cheongju and Icheon and a Silver Phoenix support team with 30 vehicles. Source: [biz.chosun.com](https://biz.chosun.com/en/en-it/2026/10/30/372GBYGCXBHK3OTEQ7YSIR6OLA/)

**FuriosaAI closes a $620 million Series D: HPCwire**
FuriosaAI said it completed a $620 million Series D to scale production of its data-centre AI inference accelerator and to accelerate next-generation silicon. Investors named in the announcement include Infinitum, Jericho Capital, QUDA Capital, Cisco Investments, Worldline Capital, the National Growth Fund of Korea and Korean institutions. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/furiosaai-secures-620m-series-d-to-meet-ai-inference-demand-and-accelerate-next-gen-silicon/)

**BrainChip launches an AKD1500 Raspberry Pi 5 kit: HPCwire**
BrainChip’s AKD1500 Raspberry Pi 5 Development Kit is available now through the BrainChip Shop. It pairs a Raspberry Pi 5 with the AKD1500 M.2 board so teams can evaluate the same chip they would design in, using PCIe or SPI. The chip is event-based, processes on the device, and supports on-chip learning of new classes without a cloud retrain. MetaTF tools and models are free through the BrainChip Developer Hub. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/brainchip-launches-akd1500-raspberry-pi-5-kit/)

**C Sun subscribes for a Nemstek stake: digitimes**
C Sun Manufacturing said on October 30 that it would subscribe for 1,900 lots of Nemstek’s privately placed common shares as a strategic investor. The expected stake on completion is about 4.68 percent, aimed at expanding advanced-packaging equipment. Source: [digitimes.com](https://www.digitimes.com/news/a20261030PD235/equipment-packaging-investment-automation-technology.html)

### Data Centres & Power
**700MW data center project proposed outside Lansing: Data Center Dynamics**
A 700-megawatt data-centre project is announced outside Lansing, Michigan. Data Center Dynamics reports that local officials were blindsided by a proposal from the local economic development agency. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/700mw-data-center-project-proposed-outside-lansing-michigan/)

**SpaceX buyout of homes near an AI data centre: Tom's Hardware**
Tom's Hardware reports that SpaceX is buying out 418 homes near a flagship AI data centre, and only from owners who drop participation in a lawsuit. The properties are supposed to house SpaceXSI staff and to give neighbours who do not want to live beside the data centre a way to sell. Source: [tomshardware.com](https://www.tomshardware.com/tech-industry/data-centers/elon-musks-spacex-buying-out-418-homes-near-flagship-ai-data-center-but-only-if-they-drop-participation-in-lawsuit-report-claims-the-company-is-targeting-an-entire-neighborhood-but-will-only-buy-from-people-who-dont-pursue-noise-pollution-complaints)

**Heim secures Omnes investment for Finland: Data Center Dynamics**
Nordic data-centre firm Heim has secured an investment from Omnes. The investment is to fund Heim’s first projects in Finland. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/nordic-data-center-firm-heim-secures-investment-from-omnes/)

**Quantum DC cancels an Australian community meeting: Data Center Dynamics**
Quantum DC’s Australian project is announced at gigawatt scale and has drawn local pushback. The company cancelled a community meeting after what it called a credible bomb threat. Source: [datacenterdynamics.com](https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/quantum-dc-cancels-australian-data-center-community-meeting-over-credible-bomb-threat/)

### Supply Chain & Policy
**CXMT plans limited HBM3E production: Semiconductor Engineering**
China’s CXMT plans to begin limited production of HBM3E soon, Semiconductor Engineering reports, citing Reuters. Manufacturing yields are put at 20 to 30 percent. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-162/)

**Vietnam’s first fab may miss a 2027 trial: Semiconductor Engineering**
Vietnam’s first semiconductor fab may miss its 2027 trial-production target, according to Reuters as carried by Semiconductor Engineering. The estimated $1.3 billion Viettel project reportedly has yet to begin construction, and talks for ASML lithography tools remain unresolved. Viettel says the project is on schedule. Source: [semiengineering.com](https://semiengineering.com/chip-industry-week-in-review-162/)

**PCB shortages projected out to 2030: TechPowerUp**
TechPowerUp, citing Nikkei Asia, says PCB shortages are projected to last until 2030. An unnamed executive at an American PC maker said some manufacturers expect orders placed today not to be fulfilled until late 2028, and that PCB supply is still short even if PC shipments fall again next year. Source: [techpowerup.com](https://www.techpowerup.com/354289/motherboard-and-gpu-prices-could-rise-further-as-pcb-shortages-extend-to-2030)

**TANAKA and MEP form a Penang refining venture: Semiconductor Digest**
TANAKA and MEP are establishing a precious-metal refining joint venture in Batu Kawan Industrial Park, Penang, Malaysia. TANAKA will hold 66.7 percent and MEP 33.3 percent. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/tanaka-and-mep-to-establish-precious-metal-refining-joint-venture-in-malaysia/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=tanaka-and-mep-to-establish-precious-metal-refining-joint-venture-in-malaysia)

### Also Today
**IQM reports full-chip entanglement on 54 qubits: HPCwire**
IQM said its cloud-accessible Emerald system has fully entangled all 54 qubits on the chip at once, with fidelity held above the entanglement threshold. Source: [hpcwire.com](https://www.hpcwire.com/off-the-wire/iqm-reports-full-chip-entanglement-on-54-qubit-quantum-processor/)

**Nagare Labs emerges with $5 million: Semiconductor Digest**
Atlanta spinout Nagare Labs raised $5 million from Playground Global to build a new memory tier aimed at AI’s memory bottleneck. Source: [semiconductor-digest.com](https://www.semiconductor-digest.com/nagare-labs-emerges-from-stealth-to-break-ais-memory-bottleneck/?utm_source=rss&utm_medium=rss&utm_campaign=nagare-labs-emerges-from-stealth-to-break-ais-memory-bottleneck)

### The Teardown: When the Night Shift Does Not Buy a Node
A process node does not move because the lab stays lit. It moves when someone can still tell a real signal from a measurement artefact, and that judgment does not stack the way wafer starts do. Wccftech’s account of TSMC co-COO and executive vice president Y.P. Chyn, speaking to students at National Cheng Kung University, is a rare on-the-record demolition of the hours theory of research.

The mechanism is simple once you separate the fab clock from the research clock. A production line gains output when a second shift loads more lots onto tools that already have a qualified recipe. Lithography, etch and deposition do not need the same engineer to be awake for every wafer. Development does. A new module is a chain of hypotheses: which film, which dose, which anneal, which defect is the limiter. The next experiment is only useful if the last one was interpreted. If the interpretation is wrong, the night crew does not buy time. It buys a second pile of wafers aimed at the wrong variable. Chyn’s line, as reported, is that research runs on brainpower, not labour, and that longer hours do not by themselves produce the result.

The worked example is the Night Owl program, from a period when TSMC was behind on process technology and trying to catch competitors. The theory inside the company was arithmetic. If TSMC’s research team worked 24 hours a day and US competitors worked only eight, TSMC would hold a time advantage and could overtake them. Twenty-four divided by eight is three. Three times the staffed hours, on that theory, should have been three times the learning rate. TSMC encouraged research engineers to take night development work so the organization would stay open around the clock. The plan was declared a failure within six months, half a year. The multiplier never showed up in the node. The missing term in the arithmetic was decision quality per hour, not hours per day. A tired team running the same mis-specified split does not converge faster. It converges on noise, and the morning team spends the next day unwinding it. That is why a 3x hours claim collapsed inside six months instead of compounding.

Chyn put the organizational repair at the 40-nanometre node. The old sequence was research finishes a process, then hands it to the fab. That handoff hit serious setbacks. The replacement, which TSMC calls One Team, is not a slogan about helping. It is shared ownership of the final result across departments. He gave two examples. First, when a new process moves from research into volume production, a longer overlap, with the fab in the development early, makes the ramp smoother. Second, when a fab hits a process problem, several teams on the root cause resolve it faster than one unit isolating the fault alone. The same rule is what he applies to fabs outside Taiwan: they cannot run as organizations fully cut off from Taiwan, and Taiwan teams have to carry some of the result. He also said getting departments to actually take that shared accountability takes a great deal of time and cannot be done with slogans.

The design choice stops being the right one when the work really is lot-limited rather than judgment-limited. A qualified recipe on a production tool, with the split already decided and the metrology already trusted, does gain from a second shift. Night Owl was the opposite case: an open research problem treated as if it were a loading problem. The moment the next wafer’s value depends on an interpretation that has not been made, adding the other sixteen hours of the day does not finish the node. It only keeps the lights on while the hypothesis stays wrong. Source: [wccftech.com](https://wccftech.com/tsmc-co-coo-chyn-longer-hours-dont-improve-rd-night-owl-program-failed/)

### On the Horizon
: Ahn Hyun’s Americas role at SK hynix takes effect.
- January 2027: Intel expects to share more on Nova Lake at CES.
- Late 2028: some PCB makers, via Nikkei, do not expect today’s orders filled before then, with tightness projected toward 2030.
